questions.question: Why is helium used in diving equipment instead of nitrogen?
questions.solution: Helium is less soluble in blood than nitrogen. Under high pressure, nitrogen dissolves in blood causing 'the bends' (decompression sickness). Helium's low solubility prevents this — divers use helium-oxygen mixtures.
questions.knowledgeNote: Helium is also used in deep-sea diving because it doesn't cause nitrogen narcosis.
questions.answer: **Why helium, not nitrogen, in diving tanks:** under the high pressures of deep diving, large amounts of any breathed gas dissolve in the blood (Henry's law). **Nitrogen is poorly soluble-but-sticky:** it dissolves in fatty nerve tissue and, on rapid ascent, bubbles out of solution — **nitrogen narcosis** (the intoxicating 'rapture of the deep' at depth) and **caisson disease/decompression sickness** (painful, even fatal, bubbles in joints and blood). **Helium is far less soluble** in blood and fat (its small, non-polar, monatomic atoms interact weakly), so it does not cause narcosis and leaves the body quickly on decompression — allowing safe deep dives. It is also non-flammable (unlike hydrogen) and chemically inert. Its drawbacks (high-pitched voice distortion, high thermal conductivity causing chill) are managed with suit heaters. **Deep point:** the choice is Henry's law applied to physiology — what dissolves under pressure must come out under pressure, and helium is the gas that barely dissolves at all.
